newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel on alert, Palestinians refuse cooperation.
newsitem.headline: Israel on alert, Palestinians refuse cooperation.

text.p: Israel went on high alert on Sunday for fear of more suicide bombings as a top Palestinian security official ruled out any immediate security coordination with the Jewish state.
Mohammed Dahlan, the Palestinian head of Preventive Security in the Gaza Strip, made a resumption of coordination conditional on Israeli implementation of peace agreements.
"We will not resume security coordination as long as Israel does not want to implement the (peace) agreements," Dahlan told a news conference in Gaza.
But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's communications chief, David Bar-Illan, said there was "no other issue than security at this point".
"Until the security issue is addressed there can be no substantive progress in negotiations," Bar-Illan said.

A leaflet issued in the name of the militant Islamic Hamas movement and claiming responsibility for a bloody suicide bombing in Jerusalem last week included an ultimatum to Israel to free all Palestinian prisoners by 9 p.m. (1800 GMT) on Sunday night.

Israeli police said the ultimatum in the leaflet, whose authenticity has not been established, was one factor in Saturday's decision to increase the number of police patrols in Israel's towns and cities.
Minister of Public Security Avigdor Kahalani and Police Chief Assaf Hefetz called on Israelis to remain alert.
Last Wednesday's suicide bombing in a Jerusalem market killed 15 people, including two attackers, and plunged Arafat's already frosty relations with Netanyahu to an all-time low.

Netanyahu has suspended peace talks, sealed off the West Bank and Gaza and signalled that he will send forces to seize militants in areas handed over to Palestinian rule if Arafat fails to do the job.

Arafat told reporters on Saturday: "The Israeli government used this situation and this incident to declare war on the Palestinian people, their National Authority and their leadership instead of declaring it against terrorism."
Speaking after talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, he said it was now more crucial than ever for U.S. President Bill Clinton to intervene to save the Middle East peace process.
Clinton announced over the weekend that he would dispatch his envoy Dennis Ross to the region to meet leaders "with our latest ideas".
Ross was due to travel to the Middle East last week but the trip was postponed in the wake of the bomb attack.

Israel's neighbour Jordan said it was worried that the Israeli clampdown went beyond tackling legitimate security concerns, warning that a heavy hand in battling militants "will only lead to more tension".
